item.title: Can We Talk About God? Why the First Page Is Blank | Fundamentals of Judaism for Beginners
item.description:
How can we speak about God at all? Understanding belief means a framework of principles. The Ramhal and Rambam define God first as the first existence, then describe His attributes, including what He cannot do, and explain how to relate to Him beyond images.

item.title: Is There a Purpose to Creation? Why the Good Must Be Earned | Fundamentals of Judaism for Beginners
item.description:
Why did HaShem create the world? The Ramhal says it was to bestow goodness, and perfect goodness exists only in HaShem. We cleave to Him according to how Godlike we have become, which is a consequence, not a reward. Gehinnom, karet and the freedom to choose all follow from this.

item.title: What in the World Is the World to Come? | Fundamentals of Judaism for Beginners
item.description:
What is Olam HaBa, and who reaches it? The soul's enjoyment of Hashem's presence, in a world of consequences where no more change is possible, after this world of choice. The class covers sins that forfeit a share, Gehinam, Gan Eden and the resurrection.

item.title: Accident or Calling? How Divine Providence Works | Fundamentals of Judaism for Beginners
item.description:
How do divine providence and chance fit together? The Rambam distinguishes general providence over the rest of creation from specific providence over people. The class covers free will and harm, whether events are accidents or callings, and why superstition and amulets take a person outside providence.

item.title: If God Is Good, Why Is There Pain? | Fundamentals of Judaism for Beginners
item.description:
Why should explanations of suffering never be offered to someone in pain? The class asks how a good, all-powerful God allows suffering, contrasting human choice with pain from God, pain as information, and turning suffering into light as Yosef did.

item.title: What Makes a Jew Different? The Kuzari and the Rambam | Fundamentals of Judaism for Beginners
item.description:
Does a Jew differ from other people in essence? The Kuzari says yes, even from birth, so that a convert cannot attain prophecy. The Rambam says no: anyone can become a disciple of Avraham or like Moshe, and chosenness is a role, with greater obligation and opportunity.

item.title: Is There Eternal Punishment? The Rambam on the Wicked | Fundamentals of Judaism for Beginners
item.description:
Does Judaism teach eternal punishment? The Rambam's view that Olam HaBa is spiritual and reflects a person's refinement, karet for the gravest cases, the soul's awareness of what it lost, and why real consequences are needed for real choice.

item.title: Is There a Misvah to Live in Israel? Rambam and Ramban | Fundamentals of Judaism for Beginners
item.description:
Is living in Israel a misvah? The Ramban counts it for all generations, and the poskim follow him, while Rav Moshe Feinstein sees it as optional. The shiur explains the Rambam's omission, the three oaths, when leaving the land is allowed, and the duty to love the land.

item.title: How Binding Is a Minhag, and Can It Change? | Fundamentals of Judaism for Beginners
item.description:
How much authority does a custom carry, and can it change? The shiur covers customs as a third body of binding authority, personal practices that have the force of a vow, communal customs, and the Beit Yosef and Maharashdam on what newcomers to a community should follow.

item.title: Did the Rambam Believe in Physical Resurrection? | Fundamentals of Judaism for Beginners
item.description:
What happens to the soul after death? For the Raavad and Ramban, the soul waits in Gan Eden until a physical Olam HaBa. For the Rambam, Olam HaBa is spiritual and begins at death, yet his Letter on Resurrection affirms a physical resurrection. Also how we reflect Hashem.

item.title: Faith and Folly: Mazal, Red Strings and Walking with Hashem | Fundamentals of Judaism for Beginners
item.description:
Is mazal real, and what about red strings and omens? The Torah forbids deciding by omens and commands walking wholeheartedly with Hashem. The class sets Rabbi Yohanan's ein mazal leYisrael against other Gemara statements, the Rambam against the Ramban on astrology, and what omens and simanim are for.
